In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stress orientation in the suprasalts is not controlled by the plate boundary forces, but by the salt diapirs.
the observed stress orientations in northern Germany are a result of the interplay of a combination of factors, including the salt viscosity, salt thickness and salt topology.
the salt-related stress decoupling is controlled by the dynamic viscosity of the salt and the geometry of salt structures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mechanical decoupling is a function of the dynamic salt viscosity, the salt geometry, the applied stress and the rheology of the surrounding sedimentary rocks.
the stress state in the subsalt and suprasalt sections of a salt basin is decoupled, and this decoupling is controlled by the dynamic salt viscosity and the salt topology.
the stress orientation in a basin is controlled by a number of factors, such as the tectonic forces applied to the basin, the salt rheology and the basin topology.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the mechanical decoupling of the subsalt and suprasalt layers is a consequence of the rheological properties of the salt and the local salt topography, and is not a function of the plate boundary forces alone.
the stress field above a salt layer is strongly controlled by salt rheology and salt topology and is therefore not necessarily the same as that in the basement.
the salt-related stress decoupling is a natural consequence of the salt viscosity being orders of magnitude lower than the rock viscosity of the surrounding sediments.
